cards.back: Development of an unspecialised cell into a specialised type through changes in gene expression. The cell keeps all its genes.

cards.front: How do embryo cells end up specialising differently?
cards.back: Gradients of signalling chemicals across the early embryo mean cells in different positions express different genes, so they differentiate.
A cell that can divide endlessly and can differentiate along different pathways.
Location in an adult tissue where stem cells are kept in reserve and their division and differentiation are promoted when needed. Examples: bone marrow, hair follicles.
Totipotent: any cell type (earliest embryo cells). Pluripotent: most cell types (slightly later embryo). Multipotent: a limited range, e.g. bone-marrow stem cells → blood cells.
No — typically multipotent, e.g. bone-marrow stem cells make only blood cell types.

cards.front: Cell size and function: give contrasting human examples
cards.back: Egg: very large (stored cytoplasm). Sperm: small, streamlined. Red blood cells about 7–8 µm; white cells larger. Neurons can reach about 1 m long; striated muscle fibres several cm.
Surface area divided by volume. It falls as a cell grows, because volume grows faster (cube) than surface area (square).

cards.front: Why does SA:V limit cell size?
cards.back: Exchange happens across the surface, but the demand for exchange depends on volume. A large cell has too little surface per unit volume to exchange materials and heat fast enough.

cards.front: SA:V of cubes with sides 1, 2 and 3 units?
cards.back: 6:1, 3:1 and 2:1 — SA:V halves as the side doubles (SA:V = 6/side for a cube).

cards.front: AHL: Three ways cells increase SA:V, with examples
cards.back: Flattening (biconcave red blood cells), microvilli and invaginations (both on proximal convoluted tubule cells: microvilli on one side, infoldings on the other).
Extremely thin, so the diffusion distance for gas exchange between air and blood is very short.
Many secretory vesicles (lamellar bodies) that release surfactant into the alveolus, reducing surface tension.

cards.front: AHL: Cardiac muscle cells vs striated (skeletal) muscle fibres
cards.back: Both have contractile myofibrils. Cardiac: branched, shorter, usually one nucleus. Skeletal: unbranched, very long, many nuclei (formed by fusion of cells), so whether a fibre is 'a cell' is debatable.

cards.front: AHL: Adaptations of a human sperm cell
cards.back: Flagellum for movement; many mitochondria for ATP; acrosome with enzymes to penetrate the egg coat; small haploid nucleus; little cytoplasm.

cards.front: AHL: Adaptations of a human egg cell
cards.back: Large, with stored nutrients; haploid nucleus; cortical granules that block extra sperm; protective coat (zona pellucida).
